newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala rebels roundly faulted for kidnapping.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala rebels roundly faulted for kidnapping.

text.p: Leftist guerrillas in Guatemala came under intense criticism on Tuesday for engineering a kidnapping that has threatened to derail a peace process to end Latin America's longest civil war.
But some critics, even as they faulted the guerrillas, urged the government to move forward with peace talks for the sake of all Guatemalans.

The government on Monday suspended peace talks planned for Tuesday in Mexico City, saying the recent abduction of an 86-year-old, wheelchair-bound woman by a rebel commander violated terms of the peace process.

The surprise government announcement came amid mounting anticipation in Guatemala that the government and the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) would sign a final peace accord in December after 36 years of war.
Left-wing members of congress, refugee groups, the United Nations, churches and business leaders all heaped scorn on the guerrillas for jeopardising peace accords.

The United Nations mission in Guatemala overseeing the peace process said the "URNG has seriously violated its commitment to respect the inherent attributes of the human being ... and has seriously jeopardised the right to life."
At the United Nations in New York, U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali was "greatly concerned," a spokeswoman said.

"He deplores this incident and the damaging consequences for the peace negotiations under the auspices of the United Nations, which are very close to a successful conclusion," chief U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa said.

The talks were thrown off track after police on Oct. 19 arrested Rafael Augusto Valdizon Nunez, also known as "Comandante Isaias," leader of one of four separate guerrilla armies that make up the URNG, on suspicion of kidnapping.

According to government officials, Valdizon admitted that men under his command were holding Olga Alvarado de Novella, 86, who was kidnapped on Aug. 25 as she left church. Kidnappers masquerading as policemen pulled over her car and overpowered her chauffeur and bodyguard.

Valdizon negotiated his freedom in exchange for giving up Alvarado, who belongs to the wealthy family that owns Cementos Progreso. The company has enjoyed a virtual monopoly on Guatemalan cement production for more than four decades.
The guerrillas have been known to raise money by abducting wealthy Guatemalans, but under the terms of peace negotiations rebels promised to end such "fundraising."

Edgar Gutierrez, an analyst of left-wing movements who works with the Myrna Mack Foundation human rights group, said the kidnapping was surprising because Valdizon's rebel faction has not been known for being radical or intransigent.
"This is a calculation error, an absolute incomprehension of the situation that the country is living in," Gutierrez said. "This shows they are politically backward.
"If the URNG doesn't give a rapid and satisfactory answer, the political situation here could polarise and we could get a violent and politically unstable period," he said.

Guerrilla commanders and government peace negotiators were to have met in Mexico City on Tuesday to continue talks regarding the political future of the URNG, one of the last topics scheduled in the peace talks.

"I hope this is really a temporary suspension so that this act doesn't really put in doubt the peace process," said Rigoberta Menchu, the Guatemalan Indian leader who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1992.
Menchu called this week's delay one of the toughest tests the peace process has faced.
